issues.failure_explanation: As written, the proposition claims the drift coefficients are determined by the solution at two time points, i.e., by two snapshots of a single trajectory (the data regime of the deterministic precursor result it generalizes). What the proof establishes is determination from ensemble means: it takes expectations of the log-modulus and of the argument of the ratios \widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\widehat u(t_1,\xi) (equations (dri-mul-ide1)-(dri-mul-ide2)), and the additive-case appendix explicitly requires two time points of the averaged solutions. The literal claim is false: from one realization, log|\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\widehat u(t_1,\xi)| = \sum_{\alpha even} a_\alpha(i\xi)^\alpha \Delta t + \sum_{\beta even} b_\beta(i\xi)^\beta \Delta W, so a_\alpha and b_\alpha\Delta W enter through the same coefficient and cannot be separated (e.g., p_1=p_2=0 gives the single scalar a\Delta t + b\Delta W for the two unknowns a and b\Delta W); the argument channel is analogous, and the small-|t_2-t_1| phase-ambiguity removal also relies on model/path information (continuous argument lift or known \Delta W) rather than on two-snapshot data. The same mismatch affects Theorem diffusion-identification-covariances, whose statement says the b_\beta are determined by two instants u(t_2,\cdot),u(t_1,\cdot) while its proof uses the ensemble ratio \mathbb E\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\mathbb E\widehat u(t_1,\xi); the paper's own pathwise propositions prop:added-1 and prop:added-2 confirm that single-trajectory identification needs extra data (the stochastic convolution or the Brownian increment).

failure_location.quote: the parameters $a_{\alpha}, |\alpha|\le p_1$, are uniquely determined by the  solution at two time points  $u(t_1, \cdot), u(t_2, \cdot)$ if $|t_2-t_1|$ is sufficiently small

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate both results with ensemble data: in the multiplicative case, parameters determined by the maps \xi \mapsto \mathbb E[log|\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\widehat u(t_1,\xi)|] and \xi \mapsto \mathbb E[Arg(\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\widehat u(t_1,\xi))]; in the additive case by the averaged solutions \mathbb E u(t_1,\cdot), \mathbb E u(t_2,\cdot) (already the formulation of Appendix sec3-appendix-prop1); diffusion coefficients determined up to the equivalence class from \mathbb E\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\mathbb E\widehat u(t_1,\xi) or the second-moment data of Appendix sec3-appendix-add-diffusion. This is a contained restatement supported by the existing proofs.
issues.overall_effect: The stated data regimes of the drift and diffusion identifiability results are stronger than what is proved: single-trajectory identification from two time snapshots is unestablished (and false in general), so the identifiability theory supports the sample-mean-based Stoch-IDENT pipeline only in its ensemble/averaged form.
issues.title: Identifiability results claim two-snapshot data but proofs use ensemble means
issues.why_classification: The repair is a contained restatement, but it weakens the stated data requirement from two snapshots of one trajectory to ensemble statistics at two time instants, withdrawing the single-trajectory guarantee; a recognizably comparable average-sense identifiability result survives, matching the paper's own 'identifiable in average sense' framing.

issues.failure_explanation: The space V is not required to be deterministic or independent of the realization and of t, so the stated existence claim is trivially true: V(\omega) = span{u(t,\omega)} has dimension 1 and gives zero error, and for prop-dis, whose target \mathbb E u(t) is a single deterministic vector, the deterministic one-dimensional space span{\mathbb E u(t)} already gives zero error since \mathbb E P_V u = P_V \mathbb E u. The proofs confirm that the constructed spaces depend on the realization (through the random coefficients c_k and on W(t), e.g., V_1 above, and likewise V_4, V_5, V_6 in the additive-case appendix) and on t, so no nontrivial statement about the approximation dimension of the data space is established. Under the only non-vacuous reading (deterministic V, as in the deterministic precursor and in lem:added-1 where V is built from fixed kernel eigenfunctions), the claim fails at t=0: u(0)=u_0 with |c_k|_{L^2} \sim k^{-\gamma} has a polynomially decaying covariance spectrum, so accuracy \epsilon at t=0 requires dimension of order \epsilon^{-1/\gamma} \gg |\log \epsilon|^2; and for prop-dis the constructed space varies with t, so even a uniform-in-t reading is not proved.

failure_location.quote: For any $t\in [0,T],$ there exists a linear space $V\subset H$ of dimension $C_{\mathcal L}|\log(\epsilon)|^2$ such that \begin{align}\label{add-over-err}   \|u(t)-P_{V}u(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega;H)}\lesssim  \epsilon (1+\|u_0\|_{L^2(\Omega;H)})\;.

Either resolution changes the type of guarantee and abandons the small-time regime (t near 0), so the advertised [0,T]-wide logarithmic-dimension data-space claims cannot be retained.

issues.why_classification: Every non-vacuous resolution changes the central quantifier (the nature of V) and the time regime: with deterministic V the multiplicative parabolic claim is false at t=0 and requires restriction to [t_0,T] with new arguments; for prop-dis no non-vacuous uniform-in-t version is established. The advertised O(|log \epsilon|^2) data-space dimensionality results do not survive as stated, and the source supports no complete repair.

Moreover, in Theorem theorem-diffusion-identification the same chain only uses 1/[(L_\epsilon+1)!]^2 \le e^{-2L_\epsilon+1} = e\cdot\epsilon with L_\epsilon = \frac12|\log\epsilon|; combined with the corrected \Theta(1) partial-sum bound this would yield only an O(\sqrt\epsilon) error, so the factorial term must be estimated properly (1/[(L_\epsilon+1)!]^2 = o(\epsilon^2) by Stirling's formula).

issues.title: Convergent partial sums bounded by a vanishing tail estimate in the O(epsilon) error chains

diagnostic_evidence.quote: K(x,y)=\int_0^T \mathbb E \left[u(s,x)u(s,y)\right]ds,\;G(s,t)=\int_{\mathcal D} \mathbb E \left[u(t,x)u(s,x)\right]dx,
&\int_0^T \mathbb E \|u(t, \cdot)-P_{V_K^k}u(t, \cdot)\|_{L^2(\mathcal D)}^2dt=\int_{\mathcal D}\mathbb E \|u(\cdot,x)-P_{V_G^k}u(\cdot,x)\|_{L^2([0,T])}^2dx=\sum_{j=k+1}^{\infty}\lambda_j.

Since $X_{s,t}(\cdot)$ is $\mathcal C^{p}$-differentiable, one can also show that $G(s,t)$ is $\mathcal C^{p}$-differentiable since $c(\cdot)$ and its derivatives up to order $p$ are bounded thanks to the compactness of $\mathcal D$.

issues.failure_explanation: Two key steps are false. (1) G need not be C^p([0,T]^2), indeed not even C^1: the flow X_{t,0} is only Hoelder in time, and time regularity of G does not follow from spatial regularity of the flow. For constant c and smooth nonconstant u_0 on the torus, u(t,x) = u_0(x - cW_t) and G(s,t) = \mathbb E[h(c(W_t-W_s))] = \psi(|t-s|) with h(z) = \int u_0(y+z)u_0(y)dy; \psi is smooth on (0,\infty) but \psi'(0+) = (c^2/2)h''(0) = -(c^2/2)\int (u_0')^2dx \neq 0, so G has a |t-s| cusp along the diagonal, and the associated integral operator's eigenvalues decay like \Theta(j^{-2}) (cusp kernel), not o(j^{-p-1}) as asserted, for any p \ge 1. The sentence claiming G 'is differentiable with respect to x' is also incoherent, since G is a function of (s,t). (2) The proof treats the eigenvalue tails of the spatial covariance operator (kernel K) and of the temporal one (kernel G) as a single sequence \lambda_j; this is false in general: in the same example the K-operator's eigenvalues are the Fourier coefficients 2|\widehat u_0(\xi)|^2(1-e^{-Tc^2\xi^2/2})/(c^2\xi^2), which decay much faster than the G-operator's \Theta(j^{-2}). The error to be bounded, with V a subspace of H = L^2(\mathcal D), is the tail of the K-eigenvalues, so the G-based decay does not apply to it.

failure_location.quote:
The differentiability of $G(s,t)$, i.e., $G(s,t)\in \mathcal C^{p}([0,T]^2)$ leads to 
$\lambda_j= o(j^{-(p+1)})$ (see, e.g., \cite{MR728689}).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Analyze the spatial kernel K directly: since u_0\circ X_{s,0}(\cdot) \in \mathcal C^p(\mathcal D) (the flow regularity already cited in the proof), K \in \mathcal C^{p,p}(\mathcal D^2), and the cited kernel-eigenvalue theorem applied to K gives \lambda_j(T_K) = o(j^{-p-1}) in dimension d=1, hence \sum_{j>k}\lambda_j = o(k^{-p}) and the stated dimension o(\epsilon^{-2/p}). For general d-dimensional \mathcal D the decay and the resulting dimension are d-dependent, so the d-independent statement must be weakened accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Lemma lem:added-1 does not establish the stated approximation dimension o(\epsilon^{-2/p}) for the hyperbolic data space; the regularity-dependent rate is unsupported, and with it the quantitative form of the parabolic-versus-hyperbolic contrast (its qualitative polynomial-versus-logarithmic content is unaffected).
issues.title: Hyperbolic data-space proof asserts false time regularity of G and equates two different operators' eigenvalues
issues.why_classification: The false steps are not typos; the conclusion is recovered in one space dimension only through a different, contained argument (direct analysis of K), and in higher dimensions the stated rate likely needs a limited weakening (d-dependence); no new global proof architecture or major loss results.

issues.failure_explanation: The first inequality of the small-time estimate is invalid: its left side is the L^2(\Omega;H)-distance between the deterministic expectation \mathbb E[u_{M_\epsilon}(t)] = \sum_{k\le M_\epsilon} \mathbb E[c_k] e^{i\lambda_k t} e^{-q_k^2 t/2}\phi_k and the random approximant w_\epsilon (which is built with the random coefficients c_k), but the right side is obtained by replacing \mathbb E[u_{M_\epsilon}(t)] with the random field \sum_{k\le M_\epsilon} c_k e^{i\lambda_k t}e^{-q_k^2 t/2}\phi_k, i.e., by dropping the expectation on the coefficients. Under the stated hypotheses one may take \mathbb E[c_k] = 0 with \mathbb E|c_k|^2 > 0; then at t=0 the left side equals \|w_\epsilon(0)\|^2_{L^2(\Omega;H)} = \sum_{k\le M_\epsilon} \mathbb E|c_k|^2 > 0 while the right side is 0, a contradiction. diagnostic_evidence.quote: $Z_N =  N^{-1/2}\sum_{n=1}^N\Phi^{-1}(p_n)$, which is a standard normal variable with  cumulative distribution function (CDF) $\Phi$ under the null hypothesis.

issues.failure_explanation: For a conventional significance level p^* < 1/2, \Phi^{-1}(p^*) < 0, so the multiplicative-noise condition 2|Z_N| \ge \Phi^{-1}(p^*) is satisfied for every Z_N (the left side is nonnegative), and the additive-noise condition 2|Z_N| < \Phi^{-1}(p^*)/2 < 0 can never be satisfied. The decision rule as written therefore always declares multiplicative noise and never declares additive noise, contradicting the section's stated purpose (detecting additive noise in order to skip the diffusion identification, as reportedly used, e.g., for the KdV experiment). For p^* > 1/2 the two conditions leave the intermediate range [\Phi^{-1}(p^*)/2, \Phi^{-1}(p^*)) without any decision. The standard two-sided rule, declare multiplicative noise iff the p-value 2(1-\Phi(|Z_N|)) \le p^*, equivalently |Z_N| \ge \Phi^{-1}(1-p^*/2), is presumably intended.

failure_location.quote: Then for some significance level $p^* \in (0,1)$, we decide that the diffusion part contains multiplicative noise if $2|Z_N|\geq \Phi^{-1}(p^*)$, and it is only additive if $2|Z_N|<\Phi^{-1}(p^*)/2$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the two conditions by the standard two-sided threshold on |Z_N| (equivalently on the p-value 2(1-\Phi(|Z_N|))), deciding additive noise when the p-value exceeds p^*; a routine correction restoring the advertised functionality.
issues.overall_effect: The additive-noise detection component of Stoch-IDENT (Section sec_stat_detect) is mathematically inoperative as written; the claimed efficiency gain for additive-noise equations rests on a broken decision rule.
issues.title: Additive-noise detection rule never detects additive noise for significance levels below 1/2
issues.why_classification: Substituting the standard two-sided normal threshold is a short, local, routine correction; no formal results or other parts of the pipeline depend on the malformed rule.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: d \rho= 5\bi  \rho_{xx} dt+ \bi |\rho|^2\rho dt+\bi  \rho dW(t)

issues.failure_explanation: With \rho = u + iv (u = Re \rho, v = Im \rho as stated in Figure fig_NLS) and real-valued W, the real/imaginary decomposition of eq_NLS is du = (-5v_{xx} - u^2v - v^3)dt - v dW and dv = (5u_{xx} + u^3 + uv^2)dt + u dW, since Re(5i\rho_{xx}) = -5v_{xx}, Re(i|\rho|^2\rho) = -(u^2+v^2)v, and Re(i\rho dW) = -v dW. The table's reference model instead assigns du = (5u_{xx} + u^3 + uv^2)dt \pm v dW and dv = (-u^2v - 5v_{xx} - v^3)dt \pm u dW: the two drift rows are interchanged while the diffusion rows are not, so the displayed reference is not the decomposition of eq_NLS under any convention \rho = \pm u \pm iv (the displayed system is instead the decomposition of a real heat-type complex equation). Every reported identified model matches the displayed reference, so as written the experiment does not demonstrate identification of the stochastic NLS eq_NLS; the surrounding claim that identification is asymmetric between the real and imaginary parts of eq_NLS is also called into question, since the true component equations are symmetric in structure.
